summary.text: A finite check establishes the required prime decompositions for \(1\le k<60\). For \(k\ge60\), set \(n=2k+1>120\); a nonzero determinant implies that some matrix entry is nonzero, yielding primes \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\), whose sum is \(2n=4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Assume the following nonvanishing conjecture for A228623:

\[
\text{for every odd integer }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne 0.
\]

We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

For a positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is

\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Here the subtractions may be read as natural-number subtractions, as in the definition of A228623. There is no truncation in the quantities in question: since \(0\le i,j<n\), we have \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\). In particular, both \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) are positive integers. By definition,

\[
a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

We first record the key consequence of a nonzero determinant. If \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne0\), then there are indices \(i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) for which both

\[
p=n+i-j \quad\text{and}\quad q=n+j-i
\]

are prime. Indeed, if there were no such pair of indices, every entry of \(M_n\) would be zero. Thus \(M_n\) would be the zero matrix. Since \(n>0\), the determinant of this zero matrix is zero, contradicting \(a(n)\ne0\). Consequently a nonzero value of A228623 supplies at least one prime pair of the required symmetric form.

For any such indices, the two numbers have sum

\[
(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n. \tag{1}
\]

This identity is valid in the natural numbers because neither subtraction is truncated, as observed above. Equivalently, one may regard the quantities as integers, cancel \(i,j\), and note that both resulting summands are positive natural numbers.

We now fix an arbitrary integer \(k>0\) and split into two cases.

First suppose \(k<60\). Thus \(1\le k\le59\). The required Goldbach decompositions in this finite range are as follows; the number before the colon is \(k\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
1&6=3+3&2&10=3+7&3&14=3+11\\
4&18=5+13&5&22=3+19&6&26=3+23\\
7&30=7+23&8&34=3+31&9&38=7+31\\
10&42=5+37&11&46=3+43&12&50=3+47\\
13&54=7+47&14&58=5+53&15&62=3+59\\
16&66=5+61&17&70=3+67&18&74=3+71\\
19&78=5+73&20&82=3+79&21&86=3+83\\
22&90=7+83&23&94=5+89&24&98=19+79\\
25&102=5+97&26&106=3+103&27&110=3+107\\
28&114=5+109&29&118=5+113&30&122=13+109\\
31&126=13+113&32&130=3+127&33&134=3+131\\
34&138=7+131&35&142=3+139&36&146=7+139\\
37&150=11+139&38&154=3+151&39&158=7+151\\
40&162=5+157&41&166=3+163&42&170=3+167\\
43&174=7+167&44&178=5+173&45&182=3+179\\
46&186=5+181&47&190=11+179&48&194=3+191\\
49&198=5+193&50&202=3+199&51&206=7+199\\
52&210=11+199&53&214=3+211&54&218=7+211\\
55&222=11+211&56&226=3+223&57&230=3+227\\
58&234=5+229&59&238=5+233.&&
\end{array}
\]

Each left-hand side is \(4k+2\) for the indicated value of \(k\), and both summands in every row are prime. For completeness, the distinct primes occurring in the table are

\[
\begin{aligned}
&3,5,7,11,13,19,23,31,37,43,47,53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97,\\
&103,107,109,113,127,131,139,151,157,163,167,173,179,181,191,193,\\
&199,211,223,227,229,233.
\end{aligned}
\]

Their primality is a direct finite trial-division check. Indeed, every number in the list is at most \(233\), and a composite number at most \(233\) has a prime divisor at most its square root, hence less than \(16\). It therefore suffices, after the evident check for the primes at most \(13\), to test divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\); none of the listed numbers greater than \(13\) is divisible by any of these. This proves the desired assertion for all \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set

\[
n=2k+1.
\]

Then \(n\) is odd. Moreover, because \(k\ge60\),

\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]

The assumed A228623 conjecture therefore gives

\[
a(n)=\det(M_n)\ne0.
\]

Also \(n>0\), so the determinant observation above applies. Hence there are indices \(0\le i,j<n\) such that

\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]

are both prime. By equation (1),

\[
p+q=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]

Thus \(4k+2\) is the sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\).

The small case \(1\le k<60\) and the large case \(k\ge60\) exhaust all positive integers \(k\). Therefore, under the stated nonvanishing conjecture for A228623, every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.
